title: The Last Newcomer
statement: A machine displays a whole number from $0$ to $100$, and it starts by displaying $0$. Each time its button is pressed, the displayed number $n$ is replaced by the remainder when $n+7$ is divided by $101$. The button is pressed repeatedly, stopping as soon as every whole number from $0$ to $100$ has been displayed at least once, with the starting $0$ counting as displayed. Which number appears on the display after the final press?
hints: Don't list the numbers one by one. Instead, try to describe the display after $k$ presses directly in terms of $k$.

Use modular arithmetic: the display after $k$ presses is the remainder when $7k$ is divided by $101$. Ask when the displays after $j$ presses and after $k$ presses can be equal, which requires $101$ to divide $7(k-j)$.

Since $101$ is prime and does not divide $7$, two displays can match only if their press counts differ by a multiple of $101$. So the displays after $0, 1, \ldots, 100$ presses are all different, and the machine stops at press number $100$. The next press would bring the display back to $0$, so ask which number becomes $0$ on the next press.
solution: Each press adds $7$ and then possibly subtracts a multiple of $101$. So after $k$ presses the display differs from $7k$ by a multiple of $101$. The display also lies between $0$ and $100$, so it is the remainder when $7k$ is divided by $101$. Suppose the displays after $j$ and $k$ presses are equal, where $0 \le j < k \le 100$. Then $7k$ and $7j$ leave the same remainder, so $101$ divides $7(k-j)$. A prime that divides a product must divide one of the factors. Now $101$ is prime and does not divide $7$, so it must divide $k-j$. This is impossible, because $1 \le k-j \le 100$. Hence the displays after $0, 1, \ldots, 100$ presses are all different. These are $101$ different values among the $101$ whole numbers from $0$ to $100$, so every number appears by the $100$th press. Before the $100$th press, at most $100$ values have been displayed, counting the starting $0$, so the machine cannot stop earlier. It therefore stops after exactly $100$ presses. The final display is the remainder when $7 \cdot 100 = 700$ is divided by $101$. Since $700 = 6 \cdot 101 + 94$, the answer is $94$. Why this works. modular-arithmetic, coprime-divisibility: the display depends only on $7k$ modulo $101$, and because $7$ is coprime to $101$, no number repeats before every number has appeared.
